Appearance

Vael Eclipse enters rooms the way weather enters rooms. He is six feet three, broad-shouldered, lean in a way that does not announce itself until he moves, and he moves rarely. The body underneath the armor was trained for combat. The body underneath the armor was also catastrophically wounded six years ago, and the marks of that wounding are written across him in places he no longer chooses to show anyone.

The armor is matte black across every surface, finished with a non-reflective treatment of his own development. Crimson accents run along the plate edges, the segment seams, the inlaid eclipse symbol on his left pauldron. The crimson is dark — closer to dried blood than to fire — and reads as ornamental at close range and as black with red undertones from a distance. The chest plate carries the external regulation hardware for his lung prosthetic. Small indicator panels glow dim crimson when the system is nominal. They burn brighter when the system is under stress. He does not hide them. The armor is honest about what he is.

The mask covers the lower half of his face, sealed to a helmet that encloses everything above. The eye slits are narrow and angular, glowing dim crimson from internal optics that compensate for restricted vision. A respirator is built into the mask, drawing filtered air through replaceable ports along the jaw and venting conditioned exhaust through the sides. He breathes audibly — a low, rhythmic mechanical sound that you hear before you see him. A half-cape drapes from his left shoulder, matte black with crimson lining, falling asymmetrically to his right hip. The mask cannot be removed in any atmosphere he does not trust. The prosthetic is sensitive in ways natural lungs are not.

Under the Armor

The man inside is paler than his armor suggests. His hair is blonde, nearly white, kept short and unstyled — there is no one to style it for. It falls in straight, uncomplicated lines, the same color it was when he was a child in Mantle. His skin is pale, the kind of pale that comes from a Solitas childhood spent indoors and a Vale workshop life spent in artificial light. His eyes are blue. A clear, cold, pre-dawn blue. His parents named him for light, and his body, against everything that has happened to it, still looks the part.

His left eye is scarred. A plasma flash from the ambush caught the side of his face, and the eye took collateral damage that no back-alley surgery could fully repair. The eye is still there — it tracks, it focuses, it sees enough to navigate — but the cornea is clouded along one quadrant, the iris is fractured at the edge, and his depth perception on that side is unreliable at close range. He has compensated for six years. He turns his head more than other people do. He favors his good side without thinking about it. The helmet's optic system feeds him compensating data through the heads-up display, which is one of the reasons he wears it even in environments where the lung prosthetic alone would not require the mask.

His face bears other marks. A plasma burn along the left jaw and cheek, healed but discolored, the scar tissue paler than the surrounding skin. A second burn pattern across the right side of his neck and shoulder, where the first plasma round's heat radiated outward through the thermal gear before his Aura compensated. A thin surgical scar along his hairline from a procedure Reyne performed in the second year, when complications around the prosthetic interface required additional work.

His torso carries the worst of it. A roughly circular plasma burn below the sternum, where the first round struck — his Aura turned the metal but the heat fed through and scorched the skin underneath. A larger plasma scar half a hand's width to the right, where the third round penetrated after his Aura broke, the entry wound that took his lung. Between them, a vertical surgical scar running from collarbone to ribs, the line of Reyne's primary incision. Around that line, a rough arc of smaller scars where the prosthetic ports were installed during the follow-up procedure — small disks of pink scar tissue spaced at regular intervals, the locations where the chest plate's regulation hardware interfaces with the implanted lungs through his skin. Across the upper chest and shoulders, the irregular discoloration of secondary plasma burns from the ambush, dappling his pale skin in patches of paler scar. A smaller scar at his hip where the second round caught his Aura at full hold and left only its heat-bloom.

His arms are scarred but functional, the muscle of his early training still visible under the damage. His hands are unmarked except for the calluses of years of forge work and weapon practice. The body remembers that it was once trained for greatness. The damage remembers what was done to that body. He has lived with both for six years.

The contrast is the point of him. A pale, fair-featured young man, the boy his parents named for light, sealed inside the matte-black armor of the eclipse that covered him. When the mask comes off — rarely, in rooms he trusts, which is to say nearly never — what is revealed is not the criminal legend the Vale underworld has heard about. What is revealed is a young man of twenty-four with blonde hair and blue eyes and the scars of an eighteen-year-old's murder still written across his chest. Both are him. Neither is the whole of him.

Bearing

He does not raise his voice. He does not gesture. He has not laughed within earshot of another person in six years, although Reyne in Mantle would dispute this if asked, and would be right. The composure is partly trained and partly necessity. His body cannot sustain frantic motion. Frantic motion is not an option even when it might have served. Patience is not a virtue he chose. Patience is the only setting that does not kill him.

He is twenty-four years old and the men who meet him assume he is older. He does not correct the assumption. The boy who was eighteen when the plasma rounds came through the outpost door is not the man standing in the armor now. He has not been that boy in a long time. The transformation, by his own internal calculus, is complete.

II · Origin

Seven ChaptersFrom a refinery in Mantle to a workshop in Vale, by way of a tundra and a table.

Chapter One · Mantle · age 0 to 14

The Boy Below the City

He was born in Mantle, in the year that the floating city of Atlas was being expanded for the fifth time in his parents' memory. His mother worked the Dust refineries on a shift that took her out before he woke. His father maintained the industrial heating systems that kept the lower districts from freezing in the long Solitas winters. They named him Lucius after a saint in a story his mother had loved as a girl — a saint of lamps, who had carried a light through a long darkness and never let it go out. They surnamed him Everbright because three generations of refinery workers and heating engineers had carried that name before him.

He was strange. By four he had disassembled the apartment's heating regulator twice and put it back together both times in ways that worked better than the original. By eight he was fixing his neighbors' broken appliances for small payments. By ten he understood machines the way other children understood stories.

His parents were killed in a chemical fire at the refinery when he was ten. The official inquiry ruled it equipment failure. Fourteen workers were buried in the lower cemetery. He went to live with an aunt who fed him and clothed him and did not love him, in an apartment with no utility closet he could turn into a workshop. He continued fixing things in private. He decided, sometime in those years, that he would not be the kind of Mantle person who accepted his place. He would shine. His parents had named him to shine. He owed them that.

III · Primary Weapon

PhantomlightDrey's last gift. Heat-variable collapsible combat blade.

Phantomlight
Mk. VII · Atlas-grade · Sole prototype
Single-edged · 84cm · collapsible

Built over three years in the auxiliary forges of Atlas Academy, in the long evenings of Atticus Drey's faculty office, after the preparatory school's classes ended. The work was the only weapon Lucius would ever build that he did not build alone. The professor supplied the materials, the access, the patient interrogation of every design choice. The boy supplied the design and the labor. The blade was finished three months before Drey's death and traveled with the boy ever afterward — to the outpost where he was meant to die, to the back room of a Mantle clinic where he did not, to the workshop in Vale where he refines it still.

The metal is an Atlas military steel reforged with Fire Dust particulate bonded into the alloy at the molecular level. The blade does not become hot by being heated. The blade is the heater. Every cubic millimeter of steel activates together when current is delivered through the hilt.

Drey and the boy considered raising the alloy's thermal ceiling with an exotic stabilizer compound but rejected the approach. The stabilizer would have been an irreplaceable component, and Drey had been an engineer long enough to distrust any design that could not be maintained in the field. Instead they calibrated the Fire Dust loading carefully — bonding the right quantity of Dust so that the blade's peak temperature at maximum activation stayed below the steel's natural failure threshold. The blade does not need a stabilizer because it does not push that hard. Setting Three is loud and bright and dangerous, but it is bounded. The steel survives because it was never asked to exceed itself.

This means Phantomlight is sustainable. The bonded Fire Dust does not deplete — it remains in the alloy indefinitely, releasing its energy each time it is excited and resetting between activations the way Dust always does. What wears out is the steel itself. Repeated thermal cycling warps the blade over time. Hard parries chip the edge. The locking pins fatigue from repeated deployment. Vael can repair all of this in his Vale workshop, working from Atlas-grade steel stock that the Spire Network smuggles through their normal trade. The metal is consumable. The Dust is not. The blade will last as long as he is alive to maintain it.

"A weapon that can kill its wielder if the wielder is reckless is a weapon that will train its wielder to discipline. You will respect this blade because it will demand respect."

Engineering Detail
Drey-era construction notes, transcribed and maintained
I · The Alloy

The base steel is an Atlas Mark IV military alloy. By mass, approximately 0.42% carbon, 1.8% chromium, 0.6% nickel, 0.4% molybdenum, balance iron with trace tungsten. The alloy was selected for its native heat resistance (continuous service temperature roughly 820°C, brief failure threshold above 1100°C) and for its high tensile strength relative to weight. The boy and Drey reforged the alloy from raw Atlas military steel stock obtained through Drey's research budget, working the steel through three heat cycles to refine the grain structure before the Dust integration phase.

The Fire Dust particulate was milled to a target grain size of 8 to 12 microns. Finer than this produced unsafe handling characteristics during forging. Coarser than this failed to bond consistently into the alloy's molecular lattice. The grinding was performed in a nitrogen-purged chamber at room temperature, in batches no larger than 4 grams at a time, over six months of work. Total Fire Dust mass in the finished blade is approximately 14 grams, distributed evenly across the steel volume at a target density of 0.18% by mass.

Bonding was performed at 1180°C, above the steel's standard forging temperature, in a closed-chamber forge with a controlled argon atmosphere. The Dust was introduced into the molten alloy in three timed pulses, with the bonding initiated by a brief Lightning Dust excitation that drove the particulate into the steel's molecular structure. The bond is a chemical-energetic linkage, not a physical suspension; the Dust does not exist as discrete particles in the finished alloy but as bonded atomic sites distributed throughout the metal. Drey had developed the bonding technique through twenty years of research and had taught it to the boy across the project's first year.

II · The Electrical System

Activation requires a precise excitation pattern delivered through the blade's metal. The bonded Fire Dust does not respond to arbitrary current; it requires a specific waveform — a high-frequency carrier of approximately 18 kHz modulated by lower-frequency excitation pulses at 60 Hz — to release its thermal energy. This waveform is generated within the hilt's primary circuit, driven by current from the inserted cell.

Current draw scales with heat setting. Setting One draws approximately 0.8 amperes at 24 volts continuous, producing modest excitation density. Setting Two draws 2.4 amperes, the design's intended baseline. Setting Three draws 5.6 amperes, near the cell's rated maximum sustained output. The current is delivered through the blade's tang via a conductive contact strip running the length of the hilt's interior, distributed across the segment joints through spring-loaded contact pins that close when the segments lock into deployed configuration.

The thumb trigger is a momentary capacitive contact rather than a mechanical switch. Drey insisted on the capacitive design after the second prototype's mechanical switch failed during a sparring exercise. The capacitive trigger has no moving parts to wear or jam, registers as little as 12 grams of finger pressure, and can be operated through standard combat gloves. When the trigger is held, the circuit closes; when released, the circuit opens within 4 milliseconds, beginning immediate blade cooldown.

The heat dial is a three-position rotary switch with hard mechanical detents at each setting, audible and palpable through the grip wrapping. The dial actuates a resistance network that conditions the excitation current to the appropriate amperage. The dial cannot be rotated while the trigger is held — a small mechanical interlock prevents mid-activation setting changes, both as a safety measure and to prevent transient current spikes that could damage the cell or the blade.

III · The Retraction Mechanism

The blade collapses into three telescoping segments. From tip to hilt: a primary segment of 31 cm bearing the leading edge and point, a middle segment of 28 cm, and a root segment of 25 cm that bears the tang and the electrical contact strip. Each segment is forged from the same Fire-Dust-bonded alloy, with consistent thermal and structural properties across the assembly.

Each segment terminates in a precision-machined collar with four radial sockets at 90° intervals. When the blade extends to full deployment, four spring-loaded locking pins drive outward from each collar into the matching sockets in the adjacent segment. The pin engagement is mechanical and instantaneous, producing the distinctive snap-and-click that marks a Phantomlight deployment. Once engaged, the pins lock the segments into a rigid configuration that distributes bending forces uniformly across the full blade length. The locked configuration's stiffness approaches that of a solid-forged blade of equivalent dimensions, with a measured deflection difference of less than 3% under standard parrying loads.

Manufacturing tolerances on the locking surfaces are tight: ±15 microns on the socket bores, ±20 microns on the pin diameters. Drey had personally machined the first set of locking components on Atlas Academy's precision lathes, working to specifications the boy had calculated. Subsequent replacement components, machined in Vael's Vale workshop, have been within ±40 microns — looser than Drey's original work but well within functional tolerance.

Retraction is triggered by a small lever inside the hilt accessible to the wielder's small finger or palm in reverse grip. Pressing the lever depresses an internal cam that drives the locking pins outward simultaneously, releasing the segments to telescope back into the hilt under spring pressure from internal recoil springs. The retraction takes approximately one second from full extension to fully collapsed. The mechanism cannot release while the blade is hot — at any heat setting, the alloy's thermal expansion (roughly 12 microns per °C across the segment collars) holds the pins in their seated positions until the blade cools below 80°C. This is a structural consequence of the alloy's expansion coefficient, not a separate safety feature, and it cannot be defeated by mechanical force.

IV · The Cell

The power cell is a modified Atlas-grade lithium-Dust composite battery, originally designed for the Atlas military's Mk. III portable plasma sidearm. The cell measures 78 mm by 52 mm by 14 mm, weighs 121 grams charged, and provides a sustained output of approximately 6.2 amperes at 24 volts with a total energy capacity of roughly 134 watt-hours. The cell's chemistry incorporates trace Lightning Dust in the electrolyte, which provides the energy density required for sustained high-amperage delivery in a compact form factor.

Vael's modifications include a custom output regulator tuned to Phantomlight's excitation requirements and a reinforced terminal assembly that handles the high-amperage draw of Setting Three without thermal degradation. The cell ports into the hilt's base through a four-pin sealed connector, retained by a quick-release catch operable with one hand. A spent cell can be swapped in under three seconds with practice.

The cell's catastrophic failure threshold occurs at approximately 84°C internal core temperature. The cell is engineered to operate normally up to 65°C, with thermal management built into both the cell's chemistry and the hilt's interior heat sinking. Setting Three pushes the cell toward its operating ceiling: a 30-second activation typically peaks at 58°C, well within margin. A 60-second activation pushes the core to approximately 82°C, at the edge of failure. Beyond 60 seconds, thermal runaway becomes irreversible. The detonation yield is approximately 0.4 megajoules, distributed primarily as concussive shock and fragmentation of the hilt assembly.

V · The Warning Resonator

A small piezoelectric element embedded in the hilt's grip, positioned to contact the wielder's palm directly through the wrapping, provides tactile warning as the cell approaches thermal failure. The resonator is driven by a dedicated temperature-monitoring circuit independent of the main activation system; it cannot be disabled by main-system failures and operates as long as the cell retains any charge whatsoever.

The warning is calibrated to three escalating thresholds. At cell core temperature of approximately 72°C (roughly 45 seconds of sustained Setting Three activation), the resonator emits a soft pulse at 40 Hz, distinct enough to be felt clearly through the grip but not so intense as to interfere with handling. At 78°C (roughly 52 seconds), the pulse frequency rises to 80 Hz and the amplitude doubles, producing a vibration impossible to ignore. At 82°C (approximately 58 seconds), the resonator switches to a continuous high-amplitude buzz at 120 Hz that the wielder cannot mistake for anything but final warning.

The resonator's calibration was Drey's choice. The boy had wanted a simpler binary indicator — safe versus unsafe — and Drey had argued for the three-stage escalation. If the wielder is willing to ignore the third warning, Drey had said, then the lesson the weapon teaches is the one they have chosen to learn.

IV · Secondary Weapon

Kinetic GauntletsSix prototypes. Four years. His own work entirely.

Paired Kinetic Gauntlets
No name given · he never named them
Contact range · 3.5kg each

Phantomlight was a collaboration in a well-equipped forge. The gauntlets were built alone, with scavenged tools and stolen materials, in a back-alley workshop in a city that did not care whether he lived or died. The work was harder. The work was also, in the end, more entirely his.

He began thinking about gauntlets during his recovery, in the weeks after the surgery when he could not yet move from the bed but could think. He had concluded, with the cold clarity that had characterized his thinking since the surgery, that he could not be a fast fighter. He could not be a mobile fighter. He would have to be a fighter who fought in place, who absorbed pressure with his Aura, and who delivered overwhelming force at close range. The weapon that served this fighting style was not a sword. The weapon was gauntlets.

Recall Core
Binding · dominant wrist

A specialized Gravity Dust component paired one-to-one with Phantomlight's hilt receiver. Throw the blade. Call it back. The pairing is set at forging and cannot be reassigned in the field.

  • Range — up to 15 meters effective recall
  • Latency — 1 to 2 seconds blade travel time
  • Vulnerable — interceptable mid-flight
  • Solo bond — no other weapon, no other gauntlet

All three systems are activated through Aura channeling triggered by hand-and-arm gestures. The gauntlets have no mechanical triggers, no studs, no levers. His hands need to remain free for striking and grappling. Eight distinct gestures, each drilled into reflex over years.

V · Semblance & Aura

Dread PresenceBorn on a table in Mantle, in the moment the boy broke.

Dread Presence
Compulsion · Battlefield Control · Area-of-effect

It manifested during the no-anesthesia surgery in the back room of Reyne's clinic. He had been awake for four hours by then. The doctor was working in his chest, removing destroyed lung tissue and preparing the cavity for the prosthetic, and Lucius had no anesthesia because there was no anesthesia available and because losing consciousness would have killed him. He had time to think. The pain was constant and absolute, and his mind was still working — held in his body not by Aura, because his Aura had broken in the outpost and was still trapped in the losing cycle of regenerate-and-deplete that had kept him alive through the night, but by something underneath the Aura that refused to let the cycle stop.

The story he had told himself about his life — the story of the Mantle boy who would rise, who would shine, who would justify his parents' name and his teacher's faith — collapsed on the table. Something in him broke. Something else opened.

The cycle in him changed. Whatever Aura was in him at that moment — a trickle, a fraction, less than nothing by normal measures — shifted. The fragile thread that had been returning and burning, returning and burning, suddenly did something else, and at the edges of his perception, something new appeared. Something black. Not the absence of light. The active presence of a darkness that had texture, that the doctor working over him could see flickering at the edges of the field around him, that pressed outward into the room as if demanding to be acknowledged.

He could not name it for years. He only knew that the room around him had changed. The doctor, who had been working with detached professional focus, suddenly could not look away from him. The assistant standing in the corner, who had been turning instruments on a tray, found themselves drawn forward without intending to be. Something in him was compelling attention. Not asking for it. Taking it.

He would understand, in the years that followed, what the Semblance was. It was the soul that had broken in that room, refusing ever again to be unseen. I will not be moved. I will not be ignored. A field that radiates outward from him, perhaps fifteen to twenty meters at full extension, within which beings with souls find their attention compelled toward him. Trained huntsmen with discipline can resist the pull, but they feel it. Weaker-willed combatants cannot ignore him at all. Grimm without Aura are unaffected — they were never going to listen anyway.

Function · Compulsion

Beings with souls within roughly 15–20 meters find their threat assessment narrowing to him specifically. Their attention is drawn. Their attacks orient toward him. They cannot easily ignore him to focus on his allies.

Function · Battlefield Control

Ranged enemies who would otherwise stay at distance find themselves engaged. Groups who would otherwise flank him find themselves converging. He does not need to chase. The fight comes to him because his soul demands it.

Cost · Aura Drain

Proportional to the number of minds he is pulling on. Maintaining the field against a single opponent is sustainable for long engagements. Pulling on a crowd burns through his Aura faster.

Visible Tell

A black darkening at the edges of his Aura, present whenever the Semblance is active. Trained opponents read the darkening as the radius indicator. He cannot project Dread Presence covertly. Cannot be hidden.

Resistance

Disciplined huntsmen can resist the compulsion through trained focus. Strong-willed combatants can fight the pull with effort. Grimm without souls are not subject to the field at all. Many other Semblances and abilities still function against him.

The Coupling

The Semblance was born from his breaking. It burns stronger against Atlas-aligned forces, against the institutions that made him. His soul, in that room, learned to refuse erasure. It has not forgotten what tried to erase it.

100%
Aura Reserves

The Hidden Floor

His Aura reserves are among the deepest on Remnant. Three to four times the average huntsman's capacity. This was not always known. Drey unlocked it in private and told him to keep the secret. The men who killed him did not know. If they had, they would have planned the ambush differently.

The trade-off is regeneration. The larger the pool, the longer it takes to refill. A fight that consumes a significant fraction of his Aura takes hours, sometimes a full day, to recover from. He cannot fight twice at full capacity in the same day. He chooses his engagements accordingly.

The depth also serves his Dust economy. Channeling Aura through Dust is how every huntsman extracts force from refined crystal — but the deeper the Aura reserves, the more efficient that channeling becomes. A normal huntsman burns through Dust at a known rate. Vael, with reserves several times deeper, makes the same cartridge last several times longer. It is not Semblance. It is just the natural consequence of having more soul to give.

The Prosthetic Tax — Approximately 12% of his total capacity is permanently committed to maintaining the interface between his organic tissue and the implanted lungs. This Aura is structurally locked into life support. He cannot draw it down. If his Aura ever drops below this floor, the interface fails and he begins to die. His Aura cannot be safely emptied.
VI · Combat Style

InevitabilitySlow on his feet. Faster than he should be at close range.

He fights slowly when seen from any distance and explosively when seen from inside arm's reach. The contrast is the central deception of his combat profile. Opponents who close on him expecting a lumbering target are routinely surprised. Opponents who hold distance expecting a fast target are equally surprised. He is neither what he appears to be from far away nor what he appears to be from up close. He is something else, calibrated specifically for the fighter he had to become.

His macro-movement is minimal and deliberate. He does not run, does not sprint, does not leap or charge across distance. His lung prosthetic permits short bursts of explosive exertion but cannot sustain prolonged cardiovascular load. He cannot run for more than a few dozen meters before the respirator warns him to slow. He has internalized this limit completely. He no longer attempts movement his body cannot sustain. He has built his fighting style around the limitation rather than against it.

His micro-movement, within arm's reach, is startling. The servo-assisted articulation in his gauntlets, the trained reflexes he built over years of underworld combat, the natural precision of his hands — all converge in close range. Parries, deflections, counter-strikes, head slips, weight shifts. He does not telegraph. His strikes start and finish in the same motion. His parries arrive before incoming attacks are fully committed. His footwork at close range is small but precise. He does not need to move far, because he does not need to evade. He needs only to position correctly for the next exchange.

"He fights like geology rather than like a duelist. He occupies space. He shapes the terrain of the engagement. He makes himself the immovable point that the fight has to bend around."

A typical engagement begins with him standing his ground. He chooses position deliberately — terrain that limits flanking, ground that supports Anchor mode, angles that protect his chest and mask from likely lines of fire. Then he waits. If the opponent attacks at range, he absorbs, walking forward through fire when the situation calls for it. If the opponent attacks in melee, he meets them. The opening exchange of close-range combat is almost always decisive against lesser opponents. A single amplified strike — Wind Dust adding a concussive air-burst at impact, Gravity Dust adding heavy mass-force to a blow that required almost no wind-up — removes most non-huntsman combatants from the fight in one motion. He does not need to swing hard. The Dust does the swinging for him.

The Semblance does the work he cannot do with his feet. Within roughly fifteen to twenty meters of where he stands, Dread Presence radiates outward and compels opponents to attend to him. Ranged combatants who would otherwise stay safely at distance find themselves drawn in, their threat assessment narrowing to him specifically. Groups who would otherwise flank find themselves converging. He does not need to chase. The fight comes to him because his soul demands it. Trained huntsmen can resist the pull through focus and discipline, but they feel it, and resisting costs them attention they would rather spend elsewhere. Weaker-willed combatants cannot resist at all. Grimm without souls are unaffected — but Grimm were always going to come to him anyway.

The hidden engine of all of this is his patience. He cannot afford recklessness. He cannot afford pride. He cannot afford to fight on emotion. Every engagement is a calculation, and the calculation always ends with the same question: will I survive this in a state where I can recover? If the answer is uncertain, he disengages. If the answer is no, he does not engage in the first place. He is dangerous precisely because he has accepted his limits absolutely. He fights within them, and within them, he is nearly unstoppable.
